summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis, hepatopulmonary syndrome, and severe asthma was admitted for acute hypoxemic respiratory failure due to an asthma exacerbation complicated by community-acquired pneumonia caused by Haemophilus influenzae. He was initially managed in the MICU with IV steroids, magnesium, and continuous nebulizers, then transitioned to the medicine floor. A CT chest revealed bilateral ground-glass opacities, leading to antibiotic initiation, later narrowed to ceftriaxone. He developed steroid-induced fluid overload and electrolyte imbalances, including hyponatremia and hyperkalemia, which resolved with diuresis and medication adjustments. His Suboxone was resumed twice daily in coordination with his PCP, and sertraline was started for anxiety. He was discharged home on a prednisone taper, new maintenance inhalers, and adjusted diuretic dosing, with plans for outpatient follow-up in pulmonology, hepatology, and primary care.
problems: Alcoholic cirrhosis of liver without ascites
Adverse effect of glucocorticoids and synthetic analogues, initial encounter
